newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL'S PETROBRAS LIKELY TO KEEP PROVEN RESERVES.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL'S PETROBRAS LIKELY TO KEEP PROVEN RESERVES.

text.p: Brazilian state oil giant Petrobras' priority is to choose what exploration areas it will keep but is unlikely to hand over to private competitors any proven or probable reserves, Mines and Energy Minister Raimundo Brito said Wednesday.

"Our priority at the moment is to determine the areas that will stay with Petrobras," Brito told a news conference marking the 20-year anniversary of oil production at Campos Basin off Rio de Janeiro's coast.
Under a new law regulating the opening of the country's oil and gas industry, Petrobras can keep those areas where it is already producing or has heavily invested in exploration.
The remainder of Brazil's 29 sedimentary basins will be turned over to a new regulatory body, the National Petroleum Agency (ANT), to be set up within 120 days at a cost of $7 million to $8 million.
"It is certainly not in the interests of Petrobras to hand over any proven reserves to the ANP," Brito said.
Brazil currently has eight billion barrels of proven oil and gas reserves and another 6.1 billion barrels of probable reserves. Most of those reserves are offshore.
Under the new law, Petrobras has drafted a list of 150 projects earmarked for joint ventures with the private sector. The projectws would require $3 billion in investment over the next three years.
Petrobras Exploration and Production Director Antonio Carlos de Agostini told reporters all joint venture projects were in areas that the company intends to keep.
He said Petrobras would only be able to sign partnership contracts with the private sector once the areas it wants to keep are approved by the government.
"Areas where Petrobras is already producing will be automatically approved but areas where Petrobras is still in a developing phase must undergo an approval process," Agostini said.
"The government can take up to six months to approve the areas to be kept by Petrobras," he added.
The most sought-after Petrobras partnerships by the private sector are in the Campos Basin, Agostini said, adding that parts of the basin would be made available for private sector development.

The basin accounts for 70 percent of Brazilian oil output of 900,000 barrels per day (bpd). Petrobras plans to invest $10 billion in the Campos Basin over the next five years to increase production from the current 630,000 bpd to 1.3 million bpd.
Company President Joel Renno said that output at the Campos Basin set a new world record drilling at a depth of 1,709 meters (5,607 feet) below sea level.
He said Petrobras plans to produce oil at a depth of 2,000 meters by the year 2000, boosting the company's prospective oil reserves.
